titre: A Blood Disease That Protects Against Malaria
accroche: In 1954, a researcher shows that being a carrier (not sick, a carrier) of the sickle cell gene protects against the most severe malaria
contenu_vulgarise:
Sickle cell disease deforms red blood cells into crescents, which circulate poorly and get stuck in small vessels. The disease, a serious one, affects those who received the mutated gene from both parents. By simple natural selection, it should therefore gradually disappear wherever it appears: so handicapping a gene is passed on less.

In sub-Saharan Africa, however, the gene does the opposite. In some regions, up to four people in ten carry it: a frequency that bad luck alone does not explain.

## What Allison goes looking for in the field

In 1954, the geneticist Anthony Allison publishes in the *British Medical Journal* the results of a survey of Ugandan children. He is interested not in the sick but in the carriers: those who received the mutated gene from only one parent, and who make both normal hemoglobin and sickle hemoglobin without developing the disease.

In these children, Allison observes infection by the malaria parasite that is less frequent, and above all far less dense in the blood, than in children without the gene. The carrier is not invulnerable: he gets infected, but the parasite multiplies less well in him.

The mechanism lies in the cell itself. A carrier's red blood cell, slightly more fragile, deforms more when the parasite settles in to feed and divide, and the body eliminates these damaged cells more quickly, parasite included, before it has had time to multiply.

## A handicapping gene that persists because of what it protects

The geneticist J. B. S. Haldane had proposed, five years earlier, that a blood disease like thalassemia could persist in a population because its carriers resisted an infectious disease better. The idea remained theoretical. With sickle cell disease and malaria, Allison gives it its first quantified demonstration in humans.

The high frequency of the gene follows the map of malaria almost exactly: high where the parasite is endemic, low elsewhere. Two opposite outcomes for the same gene, depending on who carries it: a severe disadvantage for whoever receives two copies, a clear advantage for whoever receives only one, in only those regions where malaria kills. Elsewhere, without this pressure, the same gene would be nothing but a handicap with no compensation, and its frequency there has indeed remained low.

A gene is therefore never judged on its own: its value depends entirely on the environment in which it is passed on. A study carried out in Mali more than forty years later confirms the effect with a new benchmark: in a carrier child already infected and then cured, the delay before a reinfection is, on average, about twice as long.

repere.texte: Children carrying the sickle cell trait, already infected with malaria and then cured, take on average 365 days before a reinfection, versus 184 days for children without the trait: a study carried out in Bancoumana (Mali) between 1996 and 1998, which confirms four decades later the protective effect described by Allison in 1954.
repere.source: Billo et al., “Sickle Cell Trait Protects Against Plasmodium falciparum Infection,” American Journal of Epidemiology, 176, 2012

carte.punch: Carrying the sickle cell gene, without being sick, protects against the most severe malaria.
carte.idee: Sickle cell disease deforms red blood cells and can be fatal for those who receive the mutated gene from both parents. But in those who receive it from only one, this same gene slows the multiplication of the malaria parasite: which explains its high frequency in sub-Saharan Africa.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Billo et al. (2012) — Sickle Cell Trait Protects Against Plasmodium falciparum Infection
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English, open access; confirms the effect observed by Allison with a cohort followed over two years.

quiz.question: Why does the sickle cell gene remain common in regions where malaria is endemic, according to the card?
choix: Because both diseases are caused by the same parasite
Because carrying a single copy of the mutated gene slows the multiplication of the malaria parasite, without causing the disease
Because malaria makes red blood cells already crescent-shaped
Because children sick with sickle cell disease are naturally immune to malaria
quiz.explication: A carrier (a single copy of the gene) does not develop sickle cell disease, but his slightly weakened red blood cells hinder the parasite's multiplication and are eliminated more quickly: an advantage that offsets, in these regions, the severe disadvantage suffered by whoever receives two copies.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who had proposed, five years before Allison, that a blood disease could persist in a population because its carriers resist an infection better?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card states that Haldane had proposed, five years before Allison, that a blood disease like thalassemia could persist thanks to its carriers' resistance to an infection.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the study carried out in Bancoumana (Mali) between 1996 and 1998 show, according to the card's benchmark?
choix: Carrier children are never infected with malaria
Carrier children cured of a first infection take about twice as long before a reinfection
Carrier children systematically develop sickle cell disease after an infection
The sickle cell gene has disappeared from Mali since the 1950s
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The benchmark cites the Bancoumana study in Mali: carrier children who were cured take on average 365 days before a reinfection, versus 184 days for noncarriers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which cellular mechanism explains, according to the card, the reduced multiplication of the parasite in a carrier?
choix: The carrier produces specific antibodies against the malaria parasite
The parasite cannot enter crescent-shaped red blood cells
The carrier's liver destroys the parasite before it reaches the blood
The carrier's red blood cell, more fragile, deforms more and the body eliminates it more quickly, parasite included
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that the carrier's red blood cell, slightly more fragile, deforms more under the effect of the parasite, and that the body eliminates these damaged cells more quickly.
